steps.narration: Epoch 5 sorts A:10, B:30, A:70, B:90 around the ring, giving each physical node two disjoint intervals.

production.scenario: An object-storage ring uses weighted virtual nodes so large chassis absorb more backup traffic than smaller nodes without forcing giant data moves when hardware changes.
components: Uploads hourly database snapshots into the object cluster
Terminates PUT requests and resolves object placement
Expands physical nodes into many weighted token slices
Owns many token slices because it has a denser chassis
Owns fewer token slices because it has less disk and NIC capacity
Authoritative vnode map and replication policy version
Controls token-slice movement and cutover during maintenance
flows: A backup agent writes a large snapshot object into the storage cluster.
hash object key to weighted token
The front end resolves the object key against the virtual-node map instead of assigning one token per physical node.
store primary copy on vnode owner
Because the large chassis owns more token slices, it is more likely to receive the primary for this object.
place replica on different vnode range
Replication still chooses a different virtual range so one hardware fault does not wipe both copies.
Placement changes come from the metadata DB so every front end uses the same vnode weighting.
drain only token slices affected by new hardware
When a new storage server joins, the rebalance worker copies just the vnode ranges whose ownership actually changed.
skip failed small node and remap its slices
If the small node dies, the front end remaps only that nodes virtual ranges instead of rebuilding the whole ring.
